title: Python: product services
summary: These eleven product-service modules (3,250 lines) are careful SQL services. Every create and new-version command goes through an idempotency receipt, durable writes are fenced by the run lease, artifacts publish only after a hash read-back, and routines are scheduled on database time under row locks. Comments explain invariants and cite their decisions. What raises the cost of change falls into three groups. (1) Typing stops at the seams. Connections and rows are Any (79 signatures and about 130 positional row reads in scope). Run admission takes an Any binding that three call sites fill with SimpleNamespace. Literals and models the API validates reach the application as str and dict. (2) Rules are restated instead of shared. Six receipt-and-version procedures are copied by hand. Workspace policy is loaded by 8 queries (3 here), the run-ledger SQL exists in 3 copies, agent-node detection in 4 places, and terminal run states in 3 private copies. Three stop-code lists already disagree on parent_not_running, so a pause can fail a workflow's agent node, contrary to requirement B6 ('a pause during a node stops it'). (3) A few hotspots carry most of the size. assign_tool is 134 lines with complexity 17, mostly closures that capture nothing. create_execution is 113 lines with 12 parameters, one of them unused, and read_execution is 99 lines. workflow_runner's 69-line block dispatch also depends on five private goal_loop functions through a two-way import. Would shared persistence helpers reduce the duplication without merging row and domain types? Yes. A typed connection, NamedTuple row types with explicit *_from_row mappers (the RunRow / run_from_row precedent), a receipted() helper, a next_version() helper over a closed set of tables, one workspace-policy loader and one ledger SQL fragment would all compose SQL and return rows. Domain, DTO and view types would stay where they are. Keep these helpers as narrow functions, not a generic repository (DH-06 warns against speculative frameworks). Many PLR0913 hits here are keyword-only signatures and cost little. The positional chains (7 PLR0917 hits) are the ones worth fixing.

scores.why: Passes the project's ruff and mypy strict, but falls short of DH-06 (no broad Any or untyped dicts, no duplicated business rules) and AGENTS.md canonical states: 79 connection: Any, 3 copies of the terminal states, 8 policy loaders. No size rules are configured.

Direction is domain to application to api. But 6 function-level imports (3 of them hiding cycles), workflow_runner uses five goal_loop privates, and 5 of 11 modules are both services and tool definitions.
Files are 61 to 550 lines. Most functions are short, but three run 99 to 134 lines and two exceed complexity 10 (17 and 13).
Many small single-purpose helpers (narrowed_tools, _pattern, object_path). The largest functions mix 6 to 8 steps and pass records as positional tuples.
Matches DH-03's application layer with one module per product concept. A few pieces are misplaced (approval tool models, the offload reader), and workflows.py hosts three concerns.
Durability is exemplary: receipts, leases, staged publication, skip-locked scheduling on database time. List views are N+1, and one internal call reuses a user-facing idempotent command.
Module docstrings cite PRD and decision IDs, and comments state invariants. 35 of 53 public functions are documented, with gaps at run_workflow and assign_tool, and lazy imports go unexplained.
Untyped connections and rows, an Any admission binding fed by SimpleNamespace, contract Literals widened to str, and positional tuples used as records.
Refusal codes are typed and mapped to safe errors, and causes are suppressed on purpose. But the stop-code lists have drifted and seven exception classes copy one body.
Behavior is covered by db checks (24 to 55 cases per module) and a few unit tests. Pure rules here have little fast coverage, and search and workflow_overview have no Python tests.
Correct, carefully reasoned code. Change costs more than it should because rules are duplicated across modules, typing is weak at the SQL and admission seams, and a few functions are oversized.

strengths.title: Idempotency receipts on every create and version command, with compatible fingerprints
strengths.evidence: All nine create and new-version commands in scope check and store a receipt inside their transaction (services/agent/src/autobots/application/experts.py:128-153, services/agent/src/autobots/application/routines.py:162-186, services/agent/src/autobots/application/workflows.py:154-174). Fingerprint changes preserve old receipts deliberately: workflows.py:153 says 'Only when given, so a receipt from before descriptions still matches.' Toggles, drafts, improvement decisions and owner notes (store_memory) take no receipt.

strengths.title: Staged, verified artifact publication and order-aware reconciliation
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/artifacts.py:78-123 stages a row, uploads, reads back and compares the hash, and only then publishes under the lease. reconcile_run (artifacts.py:153-157) lists objects before reading rows, so another worker's fresh upload can't look like an orphan.

strengths.title: Fenced durable writes
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/workflow_runner.py:133-148 commits each node instance in one transaction under hold_lease, with insert-only emissions. assignments.py:102-109 takes the lease and a for-share status read before admitting a child. artifacts.py:120-122 publishes under the lease.

strengths.title: Scheduling on database time, with row locks and per-routine isolation
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/routines.py:414-427 uses 'for update skip locked' and reads clock_timestamp() under the row lock, with a comment explaining why. routines.py:478-488 keeps one routine's failure from stopping the rest, and logs only the error type, per the redaction policy in services/agent/src/autobots/operations/logs.py:64-66.

strengths.title: Pure, tested decision helpers at the trust points
strengths.evidence: narrowed_tools (services/agent/src/autobots/application/assignments.py:42-67) is pure and tested in services/agent/tests/test_final_review.py:235-240. expand_groups and validate_config (experts.py:32-73) are tested in services/agent/tests/test_tool_catalog.py:148-197.

strengths.title: Workspace scoping and input hardening in SQL
strengths.evidence: Every read names the workspace (services/agent/src/autobots/application/search.py:1-3, experts.py:110, workflows.py:126). search.py:23-25 escapes LIKE wildcards. memory.py:69 uses websearch_to_tsquery, so a query can't be malformed. read_artifact (artifacts.py:219-233) takes the workspace from the row and checks the hash before bytes leave.

strengths.title: Comments that state invariants and cite their source
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/routines.py:247-249 (Decision 0026 C7), assignments.py:60 (N-4) and 104 (why the status read is under the lease), workflow_runner.py:86 (why a stop is not a failure), improvements.py:28-29 (why authority claims are refused).

strengths.title: Batched reads where they were needed
strengths.evidence: services/agent/src/autobots/application/workflow_overview.py:68-83 loads every named Expert in one '= any(%s)' query, and workflow_overview.py:18-32 builds execution summaries in one set-based statement. This is the model for fixing the N+1 list views.

findings.impact: The binding carries the run's tool grant and instructions, and its expert_id and version enter the admission fingerprint. Because it is Any, mypy strict can't compare the three namespaces with RunBinding or Inheritance. A misspelled or newly required attribute fails only at run time, on the routine, replay and workflow admission paths that only the db checks reach.
findings.recommendation: Declare the grant once in runs.py: a Protocol with read-only properties (session_id, expert_id, version, instructions, tools) and a frozen RunGrant dataclass that satisfies it. Type admit_run's binding with the Protocol and build RunGrant at the three call sites. RunBinding and Inheritance keep their own shapes and satisfy the Protocol structurally, so nothing merges. Keep the fingerprint inputs identical, and replay an existing receipt in a db check before and after the change.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: 'Avoid broad any/untyped dictionaries.' The grant is an application type. RunBinding (expert resolution) and Inheritance (child admission) stay distinct, so the contracts rule on keeping types apart holds.

findings.impact: goal_loop is the largest application module (782 lines). It can't rename or change its private finish and settle helpers without silently changing how workflow runs finish, report and keep their lease. Importing workflow_runner loads goal_loop and every tool adapter it imports. The heartbeat start/cancel scaffolding exists three times.
findings.recommendation: Make the shared run lifecycle a public module that both loops import. It holds LoopConfig, LoopResult, finish, result_of, run_status and a lease_heartbeat async context manager that owns the task's start and cancel in one place. Move loop_registry to its own registry module. Break the dispatch cycle by injection: _drive builds the child driver and passes it to run_workflow, so workflow_runner never imports goal_loop. Write the tests first (blocker_check, workflow_run_check and the goal-loop db checks), because finish and settle behavior is sensitive.

findings.title: Stop codes live in three hand-kept lists that already disagree on parent_not_running

locations.note: STOPS: 8 codes
any other non-success becomes BlockFailed, a permanent node failure
raises parent_not_running inside the leased transaction
PAUSE_FOR includes parent_not_running (line 109); NOT_OURS
STOPPING, a third list
the gateway's own running check becomes run_not_running, which is in STOPS
B6: a pause during a node stops it without failing it
the unit test lists 4 of the 8 stop codes

findings.impact: goal_loop treats parent_not_running as a wait that a person can resolve. In a workflow it is not in STOPS. Suppose the run is paused after the gateway's running check (tool_gateway.py:290-298) commits and before _create's for-share read. The agent node is then committed as failed, and after resume the run ends workflow_node_failed, contrary to B6. Every new code an assignment can raise must be added by hand to lists in three modules across two layers. This is read from code; no test covers the race.
findings.recommendation: Define the stop vocabulary once: a StrEnum plus named sets such as RETRY_LATER and NOT_OURS, in domain/tools.py or a small new module. Have assignments and the gateway raise its members, and derive STOPS, STOPPING and PAUSE_FOR from it. Add parent_not_running to the workflow's stops once a blocker_check case reproduces the pause-inside-_create race. Add a unit test that every code assign_tool can raise is classified in each set. Compare outcomes with ToolOutcome.SUCCEEDED rather than with .value strings.
findings.sketch:
# domain/stops.py
class StopCode(StrEnum):
    APPROVAL_PENDING = "approval_pending"; OUTCOME_UNKNOWN = "outcome_unknown"
    ASSIGNMENT_PAUSED = ...; ASSIGNMENT_LOST = ...; ASSIGNMENT_BUSY = ...; PARENT_NOT_RUNNING = ...
    LEASE_LOST = ...; RUN_NOT_RUNNING = ...; RUN_NOT_FOUND = ...
NOT_OURS = frozenset({LEASE_LOST, RUN_NOT_RUNNING, RUN_NOT_FOUND, APPROVAL_PENDING})
RETRY_LATER = frozenset({ASSIGNMENT_PAUSED, ASSIGNMENT_LOST, ASSIGNMENT_BUSY, PARENT_NOT_RUNNING, OUTCOME_UNKNOWN})
# workflow_runner.py
STOPS = NOT_OURS | RETRY_LATER
# test
assert ASSIGNMENT_CODES <= STOPS | PERMANENT_FAILURES
findings.ruleCheck: python-worker rule: test stale ownership, cancellation and restart where behavior changes. Treating a pause as a stop keeps the node's receipt and replays it. No lease, fence or approval is weakened.
findings.verifierNote: Traced the race: a user's pause leaves the worker's claimed lease live (runs.py:470-478), so _commit's hold_lease succeeds and the agent node is stored failed with parent_not_running, which goal_loop's PAUSE_FOR (109) treats as a wait. Read from code, not reproduced, so the recommended blocker_check case comes first. PTOL-09 in py-tools proposes the same vocabulary from the gateway side.

findings.title: workflows.py mixes definitions, execution binding and the execution read model, with two ~100-line functions

locations.note: create_execution: 113 lines, 12 parameters
policy: no caller among 17 call sites passes it, and when given, require_offered is skipped
everything after the receipt lookup is nested under 'if existing is None'
_agent_session calls the user-facing create_session with a throwaway idempotency key
read_execution: 99 lines
reads r.status again and overwrites the unused value from 454-467
status rule for unstarted instances is a nested closure

findings.impact: create_execution performs eight steps inside one nested block: version lookup, input validation, receipt, session, policy resolution with the offered check, tool narrowing, run admission and the execution insert. The API and routines share this 12-argument entry point. Its unused policy branch is a trap that would skip require_offered. The session it creates stores a receipt under a random key that can never be replayed. In read_execution the first status read is dead, and the status rule for unstarted instances can only be tested against a database.
findings.recommendation: Split the module by concern and extract named steps. Remove the unused policy parameter. Give sessions an internal insert that both create_session and _agent_session use. Return early when a receipt already exists. Make the instance-status rule a pure function with unit tests. Select current_instance and the pending-approval flag in the first query, and drop the second status read.

  executions.py    create_execution, orchestration only (~35 lines):
      _published_version(conn, ws, wf, version) -> PublishedVersion   # graph, hash, blocks, name
      execution_policy(conn, ws, graph) -> RolePolicy                 # shared loader + offered check
      granted_tools(requested: list[str] | None) -> dict[str, int]    # pure

    read_execution = _execution_row(...) + instance_views(saved, graph, current, run_status, pending)  # pure

findings.recommendation: Move the four helpers to module level. Introduce a ChildOutcome dataclass, returned both by _finished_child and by a pure mapper from LoopResult (which raises ToolFailed for paused, lost and waiting). Optionally split _create into the pre-transaction checks and the leased admission.
findings.ruleCheck: python-worker rule on replay: a finished assignment still returns its stored result and never starts a second specialist. The refactor moves code without changing that order.
findings.verifierNote: Ruff reports C901 17 at assignments.py:177; the four nested helpers reference no enclosing name, and _finished_child's (outcome, code, status, completed, remaining) tuple feeds _close's matching positional parameters.

findings.impact: Each of the six repeats the receipt lookup, lock, not-found and conflict checks, insert, latest_version bump and receipt store. Each builds the receipt scope as a positional 5-tuple whose operation and target strings can be swapped without a type error. The copies already diverge: create_session fingerprints resolved versions, so an honest retry with the same key after an Expert gains a version is refused as idempotency_conflict, whereas create_expert fingerprints the request.
findings.recommendation: Yes, shared persistence helpers would remove this without merging row and domain types. First, a ReceiptScope NamedTuple and a receipted helper that opens the transaction, takes the advisory lock and returns either the prior result or a store callback. Second, a next_version helper for the lock, check and bump step over a closed set of parent tables (composed with psycopg.sql.Identifier). It raises a typed conflict that each module maps to its own code. Each module keeps its own INSERT, row type and view mapping. Always fingerprint the request, never resolved state, and fix create_session accordingly; its old receipts mismatch once, then expire under retention. Keep the helpers narrow: no generic repository layer.

Excerpt from routines.py:354-361. Counted with grep 'default_profile, role_overrides from app_private.model_policies' over services/agent/src: 8 sites, 3 in this area. Grep 'i.root_run_id = r.id or i.run_id = r.id' finds 3 ledger statements.
findings.impact: The role policy a run is admitted with (MP-01's order) and the money a list shows are business rules, and every copy must change together. The workflow preview computes the executor model separately from create_execution, and the two already differ: the preview applies the Expert's role bindings, while an agent step's child run inherits the workflow run's snapshot, which create_execution resolves without them. The three ledger copies must also agree on which invocation statuses count as reserved.
findings.recommendation: Add one application function, workspace_role_policy(connection, workspace_id, *, run_overrides=None), plus require_offered_policy, and use it in routines, workflows, workflow_overview and the API. Add a helper that turns an ExpertConfig into overrides, replacing the comprehension repeated four times in scope. Decide whether an agent step's model comes from the Expert's bindings or from the workflow's snapshot, and have the preview and admission call the loader the same way; WF-03 doesn't say, so raise it as a question. Share one ledger SQL fragment between run_projection and workflow_overview, or add a view through a forward migration.
